title: CalHFA Down Payment Assistance: What CA Buyers Should Know
description: CalHFA programs help eligible California buyers with down payments and closing costs. Here's how they work, the trade-offs, and how to check availability.
image_alt: A hand holding house keys above small model houses

faq.a: The California Housing Finance Agency is the state's affordable housing lender. It offers first mortgage programs and down payment and closing cost assistance through approved lenders.
Most CalHFA assistance is structured as a deferred junior loan, meaning no monthly payment but repayment when the home is sold, refinanced, or paid off. Terms vary by program.

faq.q: How do I know if a program is currently open?
faq.a: Funding and program windows change. Check CalHFA's website and ask a CalHFA-approved lender for current availability.

body_html:
Saving for a down payment is the biggest hurdle for most first-time buyers in California. The California Housing Finance Agency, or CalHFA, exists to help with exactly that. Its programs aren't the right fit for everyone, but for eligible buyers they can turn "someday" into "this year."

Here's how the main programs work in general terms. Always confirm current details, because funding, limits, and windows change.

How CalHFA works

CalHFA doesn't lend directly to the public. Instead, you work with a CalHFA-approved lender who originates a CalHFA first mortgage and pairs it with assistance. Eligibility typically depends on income limits, sales price limits, completing homebuyer education, and occupying the home as your primary residence. The full, current guidelines live on CalHFA's homebuyer programs page.

The main types of assistance

Program typeWhat it helps withHow it's repaid
MyHome AssistanceDown payment and/or closing costsDeferred junior loan, repaid on sale, refinance, or payoff
Zero Interest Program (ZIP)Closing costs, paired with certain first mortgagesDeferred, no interest
Dream For AllA larger share of the purchase price for qualifying first-generation buyersShared appreciation: repay the amount plus a share of the home's value gain

Dream For All has historically opened in limited funding rounds, sometimes with a registration window and a lottery. If you're interested, watch for announcements well ahead of time.

Who tends to be a good fit

  • First-time buyers with steady income who are short on down payment savings
  • Buyers whose income falls within the county's CalHFA limits
  • Buyers comfortable with a junior loan that's repaid later
  • First-generation homebuyers, for programs that prioritize them

Trade-offs to understand

Assistance isn't a grant in most cases. A deferred junior loan means you'll repay it when you sell or refinance. Shared appreciation programs mean giving up part of your future equity. CalHFA first mortgage pricing may also differ from what you'd get without assistance. None of that makes these programs a bad deal, but it does mean comparing the total picture against other options, like family gift funds or a standard low down payment loan.

Steps to get started

  1. Check eligibility. Look up the income and sales price limits for your county.
  2. Complete homebuyer education. Required for most programs, and genuinely useful.
  3. Work with an approved lender. Ask directly whether the lender originates CalHFA loans and how often.
  4. Get pre-approved with the program in mind. Your pre-approval should reflect the exact program you'll use.
  5. Plan for timing. Assistance can add steps to escrow, so build that into your offer timeline.

How assistance changes your numbers

It's worth seeing how assistance fits into a purchase in practical terms. With a deferred junior loan, the assistance reduces the cash you need to bring to closing. Your monthly payment is typically based on your first mortgage, since many deferred programs don't require monthly payments on the assistance. The trade-off shows up later, when you sell or refinance and repay the assistance.

QuestionWhy it matters
How much cash will I need at closing?Assistance often lowers this significantly
What's my total monthly payment?Compare against the same home without assistance
What will I repay later, and when?Affects your equity when you sell or refinance
Does the program limit refinancing?Some structures make future refinancing more complex

Local programs can stack

Beyond CalHFA, some cities and counties in Southern California offer their own down payment assistance, often for buyers working or living in the area. These programs have their own rules, funding cycles, and waiting lists. In some cases they can be combined with state programs. Ask your loan officer which local options are active where you're shopping, and check eligibility early, since funding can be limited.

The best approach is to compare two or three structures side by side: a standard low down payment loan, the same loan with assistance, and, if available, a combination with a local program. Seeing them together makes the trade-offs clear.

The takeaway

CalHFA programs can bridge the gap between what you've saved and what you need to buy. Understand how repayment works, compare the full cost against other paths, and confirm current availability before you count on it. A quick conversation with a loan officer who knows these programs can tell you in minutes whether you're likely to qualify.
